stomach noun

also tummy (the organ), on an empty stomach, upset stomach, stomach trouble, digestion

classical

Cels. 1.8: stomachō labōrāre (Lewis & Short)
Hor. S. 2.2.18
Traupman 59

stomachus, stomachī m.

noun, second declension

Properly the gullet (Cic. N.D. 2.135), then, commonly, the stomach. It also means taste, liking (lūdī nōn tuī stomachī, Cic. Fam. 7.1.2) and, often in Cicero’s letters, irritation (see be-cross). “To have stomach trouble” is stomachō labōrāre (Traupman 66).

Other words

  • venter, ventris m. — belly; stomach

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Traupman 59

    The belly as a whole, and the stomach as what is full or empty (see belly).

  • ventriculus, ventriculī m. — stomach

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Cels. 4.1.12; Plin. NH 11.200 (Lewis & Short); M-O s.v. stomach

    Diminutive of venter; the medical writers’ word for the stomach; ventriculus cordis is a ventricle of the heart (Cic. N.D. 2.138).

Examples

  • cum sale pānis lātrantem stomachum bene lēniet

    bread with salt will soothe a growling stomach nicelyHor. S. 2.2.17–18

  • fastīdientis stomachī est multa dēgustāre

    tasting lots of things is the mark of a fussy stomachSen. Ep. 2.4

  • ōrātiōnem Graecam Latīnamve clārē et intentē nōn tam vōcis causā quam stomachī legō

    I read a speech in Greek or Latin loudly and with effort, not so much for my voice as for my digestionPlin. Ep. 9.36.3

  • stomachō labōrāre

    to have stomach troubleTraupman 398

See also belly, tummy ache, bowels, be cross.
